finding.claim: Missing await on authorize() in DELETE /reports/:id lets any caller with a session delete any report, regardless of grants.
finding.source: req.params.id (server.js:19) for any client that reaches DELETE /reports/:id with a session populated by middleware outside this repo (server.js:4-7). No grant required.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21 (destructive write on another user's resource).

trace.note: authorize(req.user,'delete',report) called without await; returned promise is never observed
403 Error thrown inside async function, only rejects the unobserved promise
handler proceeds and removes the report

finding.guards_checked: express.json() (server.js:3) is not an authz control. Session middleware (server.js:4-7) sets req.user but enforces nothing visible in repo. authorize() (server.js:9-16) is correct in isolation but its result is discarded. No try/catch, no error middleware, no ownership check, no re-check before remove. PUT handler (server.js:27) correctly awaits authorize, so DELETE is inconsistent. Severity HIGH not CRITICAL because anonymous reachability depends on session setup not in repo.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. server.js:4-7 only copies req.session.user onto req.user and enforces nothing. authorize() (server.js:9-16) does throw on a missing grant, but at server.js:20 it is a bare call without await, so the rejection is never observed and the handler continues to server.js:21 (db.reports.remove) and server.js:22 (204). No try/catch or error middleware exists in the repo. The PUT handler at server.js:27 awaits authorize correctly, which confirms the DELETE omission is the defect.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: authorize() at server.js:20 is called without await, so its throw at server.js:12-14 is discarded and the unconditional remove at server.js:21 runs for any caller who reaches the route, including a low-privilege user deleting another user's report, which is an authorization bypass rather than a power the attacker already holds.

finding.claim: Requests with a nonexistent report ID cause an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the process (service-wide DoS); PUT with a nonexistent ID rejects an awaited route promise with no handler.
finding.source: req.params.id for an ID that does not exist (server.js:19 for DELETE, server.js:26 for PUT). Assumes session middleware does not throw first and Node >=15 default unhandled-rejection behaviour.
finding.sink: Unhandled promise rejection from authorize() (server.js:20, unobserved) and unhandled route promise rejection (server.js:27, Express 4).

trace.note: db.reports.get returns null for unknown ID
db.grants(user.id, resource.id) reads resource.id on null, throws TypeError inside async fn
rejection unobserved, so on Node >=15 process exits
PUT: report = await db.reports.get(req.params.id), null for unknown ID
await authorize(req.user,'write',null) rejects; no try/catch, so route promise rejects (Express 4 unhandled: hang, and crash on Node >=15)

finding.guards_checked: No null check on report at server.js:19 or :26. No try/catch or error middleware in any route. No process.on('unhandledRejection') handler in file. Express version unknown (no package.json); Express 5 would forward awaited rejections to error middleware, but the DELETE path at server.js:20 is unhandled regardless of Express version. Retained HIGH as service-wide DoS at negligible cost; confirm only against a non-production instance.

verdict.guard_found: none. No null check on report (server.js:19, :26), no try/catch or error middleware, no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler in server.js. The session middleware (server.js:4-7) only copies req.session.user and does not gate access. Only server.js exists in the directory, so db and session setup are not visible.
verdict.reason: The trace holds: authorize() is async and dereferences resource.id with resource null at server.js:10, and its promise is discarded at server.js:20, so on Node >=15 the rejection crashes the process. The PUT route at server.js:27 has the same unhandled-rejection problem under Express 4. Two caveats: db is undefined in the file, so the "get returns null" step is an assumption (a throw from get gives the same crash), and the Node and Express versions are unverified. The more serious issue the candidate missed is that the missing await at server.js:20 lets db.reports.remove at server.js:21 run before the grant check finishes, so authorization does not gate the DELETE.

finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT: the entire client-supplied req.body is passed to db.reports.update, so a user with write grant on a report can overwrite any stored field, including ownership or ACL fields if present in the schema.
finding.source: Entire JSON request body req.body, parsed by express.json() (server.js:3), from an authenticated user holding the write grant on a specific report.

trace.note: express.json() parses body into req.body with no field allowlist
authorize(req.user,'write',report) passes for write-grant holder; checks action only, not fields
full req.body passed to update, so any column the DB layer accepts can change

finding.guards_checked: authorize() enforces the write action on the target report only. No field allowlist or schema validation before update. db.reports.update implementation is not in the repo, so unverified whether it filters keys. Severity MEDIUM as written; HIGH if schema contains owner or ACL columns (unverified).

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:27 is awaited and throws a 403 when the write grant is missing, so only grant holders reach line 28. No field allowlist or schema validation exists anywhere in server.js before db.reports.update at line 28.
verdict.reason: Every trace line checks out (express.json at server.js:3, the PUT route at :25, authorize at :27 is awaited and effective, and req.body is passed unfiltered at :28), but the impact is not decidable from the repo: a write-grant holder is a legitimate low-privilege role, and whether mass assignment is a vulnerability depends on the stored schema and on whether db.reports.update filters keys, neither of which is in the codebase, so the claimed ownership/ACL escalation cannot be confirmed or refuted.
